1.goal: To open without saying that the lesson is about question form.
1.interaction: T–S, one line from you and straight on.
run: Do not announce the object. Stage 2 is diagnostic and only works if she does not know what you are measuring.
1.support: If she asks what today is about, say it is the other half of a conversation, and move.
1.challenge: None here — anything extra tells her what you are measuring.
1.monitoring: Whether she starts preparing forms in her head.
1.evidence: Nothing yet. The sample starts on the next screen.
1.transition: Move on when she is on the next screen.

2.goal: To see whether she can produce the question on her own, with no support and no warning.
2.interaction: T answers; S has to find the question. Three rounds.
run: YOU answer and she has to work out the question. Say the answer below and wait.
Three answers, three questions.
CORRECT NOTHING HERE. Note the form she uses: it is the baseline of the day.
exact: In a public school, in São Paulo.
2.expected: Three attempts, however malformed. The form is the measurement, not the content.
2.support: If nothing comes at all, say the answer again more slowly. Do not offer the question.
2.challenge: Give a fourth answer that could come from two different questions.
2.monitoring: Which form she reaches for: inversion, a question word, or a statement with rising intonation.
2.evidence: The three attempts. They are the baseline, and they come back at stage 4.
2.transition: Move on when she has risked all three, however malformed.

3.goal: Six exchanges on screen, with the questions removed.
3.interaction: S matches alone; you discuss only the misses.
run: She matches each answer to a question. Discuss only the ones she gets wrong.
The answer already gives the question away. That is half the form, and she already recognizes it — tell her so.
exact: “Yes, we do” answers a question starting with what? (Do.) And “No, I am not”? (Are.)
3.expected: Six matched, with the two CCQs answered.
3.support: If a match resists, read the answer out loud and ask what the first word of the question has to be.
3.challenge: Ask her to write a seventh answer and the question that goes with it.
3.monitoring: Whether she uses the answer as evidence, or guesses.
3.evidence: That she already reads the form backwards from the answer. It is the bridge to stage 4.
3.transition: Move on when the six are matched.

4.goal: For HER to find what separates a question from a statement with a question mark.
4.interaction: S marks on screen, then T–S until she words it.
run: She marks the three that are question form.
Then ask what is at the front of the three she chose.
DO NOT GIVE THE RULE. It comes at stage 5, afterwards.
Accept the wording in Portuguese and give it back in English.
exact: What is at the front of the three you chose?
4.expected: The answer you want, from her: something moved — do, are, or the question word came to the front.
4.support: If it will not come, read one question and one statement back to back and ask what changed place.
4.challenge: Ask her to turn one of the statements into a question without adding any word.
4.monitoring: Whether she names movement, or just intonation. Movement is the form.
4.evidence: Her own wording of what moves.
4.transition: Move on when she has said what changes place.

5.goal: The whole form, once, in one line — AFTER the attempt.
5.interaction: T–S over the table, then two CCQs.
run: Show it, read it with her, and move on. Two minutes, not seven.
She has a doctorate in Education. Say WHY the rule came after the attempt — that interests her, and it is what sustains the buy-in.
exact: “Do you like your school?” or “Are you like your school?” (Do — it is an action.)
And “___ you tired?” (Are — it is a state.)
Why the order: “You tried first, and then you saw the form. That order is on purpose: the rule stays because you already needed it.”
5.expected: Both CCQs answered, and the do/are split clear.
5.support: If the split blurs, give two more pairs quickly rather than explaining.
5.challenge: Ask for one question of each type about your own week.
5.monitoring: Whether the rule lands as confirmation of what she just did, or as new material.
5.evidence: Nothing new here — the measure is in the drill and in the free turn.
5.transition: Move on when the two CCQs are answered.

6.goal: Speed: the question has to come out without being assembled.
6.interaction: T gives the subject; S makes the question immediately. Twelve, fast.
run: Twelve questions, fast. You give the subject (“school”), she makes the question.
Immediate, gentle correction, in one word: Do. No explanation.
COUNT THE HITS. It is half the evidence of the day.
6.expected: Twelve questions, with the hit count written down.
6.support: Shorten the subject rather than explaining. One word is enough.
6.challenge: Alternate action and state subjects without warning.
6.monitoring: The hit rate, and whether it improves across the twelve.
6.evidence: The number of hits out of twelve. Half the evidence of the lesson.
6.transition: Move on when the twelve have gone by.

7.goal: Her own questions, with the six exchanges still on screen.
7.interaction: S asks you six questions, one at a time; you still correct.
run: She asks you six questions, one at a time, about work.
Here you still correct.
If she uses the real names of her school, accept it — the real content is worth more.
exact: The first word, when the question stalls: “Do…” · “Are…” · “What…” — and nothing more.
7.expected: Six questions of her own, each answerable.
7.support: If a question stalls, give the first word (Do / Are / What) and let her build the rest.
7.challenge: Answer one of them with a single word and see whether a follow-up comes.
7.monitoring: Whether the form holds when the content is hers and she cares about the answer.
7.evidence: How the hit rate compares with the drill, before the screen comes off.
7.transition: Move on when the six have come out.

8.goal: The production of the lesson — six questions in a row, with nothing on screen.
8.interaction: Role-play. You are someone she has just met at the meeting.
run: CLOSE THE SIX EXCHANGES ON THE SCREEN.
She asks six questions in a row, and at least two of them have to be born from the previous answer.
DO NOT CORRECT DURING. The conversation is hers.
Record it. It is the first time she runs a conversation in English.
8.expected: Six questions, at least two of them following from what you just said.
8.support: If she runs out after three, answer with something that opens a door and wait.
8.challenge: Give an answer that contradicts something you said earlier and see whether she notices.
8.monitoring: IF THE SIX COME OUT EASILY, that is the finding: the problem is not the form, it is speaking in a group — and that changes the design of lesson 12. Note it.
8.evidence: How many of the six were born from the previous answer. That is the number that counts.
8.transition: Move on when the six have come out, or at five minutes.

9.goal: To hand back two points and to ask for the same six to a different person, in half the time.
9.interaction: T–S, two short points, then one retask.
run: Two things, short.
Count the questions out loud with her and say how many were born from the previous answer — that is the one that counts.
Then: the same six to a different person, in half the time.
Do not add new content.
exact: Same six, someone else — and half the time. Which two do you keep?
9.expected: Two or three questions kept, and the follow-ups surviving the cut.
9.support: If she keeps only the opening ones, ask which answer she actually wanted.
9.challenge: Cut it again to two questions and ask which single one she would spend.
9.monitoring: Whether the questions born from the answer are the ones she keeps, or the first to go.
9.evidence: What she kept. It goes in the record and is read at lesson 12.
9.transition: Move on when the shorter round has been done.

10.goal: To register what was worked on and to leave the next lesson announced.
10.interaction: S ticks the list; T–S on the close.
run: She ticks what she recognizes.
Homework, said out loud and never on screen: the post-class has one optional recording of six questions to someone real, and the six questions for the November meeting written out.
Announce lesson 12: it closes the block — she joins a meeting, says who she is, asks two questions and answers one she did not see coming.
exact: Next time: four people on a call, and nobody says your name. It is the Meteoro meeting, made small.
10.expected: Some lines ticked, and one honest answer on the confidence row.
10.support: If nothing is ticked, ask which of her six questions she would ask a real colleague this week.
10.challenge: Ask who she will ask a question to before the next lesson.
10.monitoring: Whether the confidence mark tracks the drill or the free conversation. The gap is the lesson.
10.evidence: Fill today's record BEFORE you close. The next lesson closes the block and reads the four together.
